newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor to seek further 1997 budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor to seek further 1997 budget cuts.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor said on Tuesday he would seek to cut the 1997 budget by a further two billion shekels on top of the 4.9 billion shekels already proposed.
"We estimate that we are short on the income side for 1997 an amount that could reach two billion shekels," Meridor said.

The minister would not say when he would ask parliament to approve the additional cuts nor would he say where he would make them. A senior government official said on Monday that additional cuts would not be made to the defence budget.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has indicated in the past that additional cuts may be needed.

"I want to be sure as possible about the amount needed," Meridor said. "If we know enough before the conclusion of the current (parliamentary) debate, we will do it this year. If not, we will do it next year. But that's a technicality. There is no doubt that there is a need for this additional cut."
He said the income situation would become clearer in another 11 days when November revenue figures are in.

Meridor already faces considerable opposition in parliament to the 4.9 billion shekel cut, even among the ruling coalition members. Parliament is now debating the budget and has until December 31 to approve it.

Opponents say the reductions will hit lower-income groups hardest and earlier this week the parliamentary finance committee rejected a Treasury plan to impose a means test on child allowances. The test was intended reduce the number of beneficiaries and save 650 million shekels.
On Tuesday, Meridor criticised parliament for failing to act on the cuts.

"Unfortunately, some decision makers, and I see this in the parliament, understand everything I say (about the need for spending cuts), but there isn't always a direct connnection between their understanding and their voting behavior," he said.
"Everyone supports the cuts but not from their own budget," he said.

The Treasury aims to keep next year's deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, after breaching its target in each of the last two years. This year government revenues have fallen behind projections, which has widened the 1996 budget deficit and will affect the 1997 revenue outlook.

Meridor warned that parliament's failure to approve the spending cuts would have severe effects on the economy. Israel's current account deficit is expected to widen to approximately $5 billion this year from $4.1 billion in 1995.
"If the cuts are not approved and the budget deficit widens, we will need to take loans and there will be a worsening of the (current account) deficit," he said. "It will be harder to raise money."
He also raised the spectre of renewed inflation, fed by a depreciating shekel, and warned that low-income groups would suffer the most from a deteriorating economy.
